questions.title: What is the bias-variance tradeoff, and how do you tell which one dominates your current model?
questions.content: Explain the bias-variance decomposition, then describe how you would use learning curves in a real project to decide whether a model is underfitting or overfitting.
questions.referenceAnswer: Bias measures how far the model's assumptions sit from the true relationship; variance measures sensitivity to perturbations in the training set. Total error decomposes into bias squared + variance + irreducible noise. To diagnose: plot training and validation error against training set size or model complexity. If both are high and close together, you have high bias (underfitting) — increase model capacity or add features. If training error is low but validation error is much higher, you have high variance (overfitting) — add data, add regularization, or reduce capacity.

questions.title: Why does L1 regularization produce sparse solutions while L2 does not?
questions.content: Explain from both a geometric and a gradient perspective why L1 drives weights exactly to zero and L2 does not.
questions.referenceAnswer: Geometrically, the L1 constraint region is a diamond whose vertices sit on the coordinate axes, so the loss contours are most likely to touch it at a vertex, driving some weights to exactly zero. The L2 region is a sphere — smooth everywhere — so the tangent point generally does not land on an axis. From the gradient side, the L1 subgradient near zero is a constant plus or minus lambda, which pushes small weights all the way to zero and holds them there. The L2 gradient is 2*lambda*w, which shrinks as w shrinks, so it approaches zero asymptotically but never arrives.

questions.title: With severe class imbalance, should you look at ROC-AUC or PR-AUC? Why?
questions.content: You are evaluating a binary classifier where the positive class is 0.1% of the data. Which metric do you trust, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Use PR-AUC. The ROC x-axis is FPR = FP/(FP+TN); when negatives vastly outnumber positives, TN dominates the denominator, so even a large absolute number of false positives yields a tiny FPR. The ROC curve looks great and hides the real problem. The PR curve uses precision and recall, both of which depend only on positives and false positives, so it is not diluted by the huge TN count. Worth adding: ROC-AUC is insensitive to class prior, which helps when comparing across datasets; PR-AUC shifts with the positive rate, so only compare it within the same distribution.

questions.title: Why can't you use random splits for cross-validation on time series data?
questions.content: Explain what goes wrong with random K-fold on time series, and describe the correct approach.
questions.referenceAnswer: Random splitting puts future data in the training set and past data in validation, which leaks information and produces wildly optimistic estimates that collapse in production. The correct approach is a temporal split: sort by time, then use walk-forward or expanding-window validation so the training set always precedes the validation set. Also watch feature engineering — any rolling-window statistic must be computed using only data available before the split point.

questions.title: What is data leakage? Give three examples that are easy to miss in practice.
questions.content: Define data leakage and give three subtle but common sources of it in a real modeling pipeline.
questions.referenceAnswer: Data leakage is using information during training that would not be available at prediction time, which inflates offline metrics. Common examples: (1) Standardizing or imputing on the full dataset before splitting, so test-set statistics leak into training. (2) A feature that is a downstream artifact of the label — for example, using 'refund issued' to predict 'is fraud'. (3) Samples from the same user or entity split across train and test, so the model memorizes entities rather than learning the pattern; use grouped splits by entity instead.

questions.title: Why does Batch Normalization use running statistics at inference time?
questions.content: Explain how BN behaves differently in training versus inference, and why you cannot simply use the current batch statistics at inference.
questions.referenceAnswer: During training BN normalizes with the current mini-batch mean and variance while accumulating a running average. At inference you must use the running average for three reasons: (1) Inference is often single-sample or very small batch, where batch statistics are extremely noisy or undefined. (2) Using current-batch statistics makes a sample's prediction depend on whichever other samples happen to share its batch, destroying determinism. (3) The normalization distribution must match between training and serving, otherwise you get train/serve skew.

questions.title: How does Layer Normalization differ from Batch Normalization, and why do Transformers use LN?
questions.content: Compare the axes each normalization operates over, and explain the reasons Transformers chose LN.
questions.referenceAnswer: BN computes mean and variance per feature channel across the batch dimension, so it depends on batch size. LN normalizes across the feature dimensions of a single sample, independent of batch. Transformers use LN because: (1) NLP sequences are variable length, and padding contaminates BN's batch statistics. (2) Batches are often small during training and inference is frequently single-sequence, making BN statistics unstable. (3) LN normalizes each token independently, which fits autoregressive decoding naturally and introduces no cross-sample dependency.

questions.title: What is the complexity of self-attention, and what are the main approaches to reducing it?
questions.content: State the time and space complexity of standard self-attention with respect to sequence length, then list at least three families of optimization.
questions.referenceAnswer: Standard self-attention is O(n^2 * d) in time and O(n^2) in space for the attention matrix, where n is sequence length. Optimization families: (1) Sparse attention — compute only local windows or strided patterns, as in Longformer and BigBird. (2) Linear attention — approximate softmax with a kernel so associativity lets you compute K^T V first, giving O(n * d^2), as in Performer. (3) IO-aware exact implementations — FlashAttention does not change the math but tiles the computation and never materializes the n-by-n matrix, dramatically cutting memory traffic. (4) Retrieval or compression approaches that condense long context into a small number of summary tokens.

questions.title: What causes vanishing and exploding gradients, and how do modern networks mitigate them?
questions.content: Explain both phenomena starting from the chain rule, then list the mitigations used in practice.
questions.referenceAnswer: During backpropagation the gradient is a product of per-layer Jacobians. If the relevant singular values are consistently below one the product decays exponentially (vanishing); consistently above one and it grows exponentially (exploding). Mitigations: residual connections give gradients an identity path; normalization layers (BN/LN) stabilize the distribution of layer inputs; proper initialization (He/Xavier) preserves variance forward and backward; ReLU-family activations avoid the saturation regions of sigmoid; gradient clipping caps explosion directly; and in RNNs, LSTM/GRU gating preserves long-range gradient flow.

questions.title: What does Adam buy you over SGD, and what does it cost? When would you still pick SGD?
questions.content: Compare the two optimizers and explain when momentum SGD is the better choice.
questions.referenceAnswer: Adam maintains exponential moving averages of the first and second moments to adapt per-parameter learning rates. It converges quickly, is relatively insensitive to the learning rate, and handles sparse gradients and large language models well. Costs: optimizer state roughly doubles parameter memory; on some vision tasks generalization is slightly worse than SGD; and adaptive scaling interacts badly with weight decay, which is why AdamW decouples them. Pick momentum SGD when you want best-in-class generalization on CV classification, when memory is tight, or when reproducing a classic baseline.

questions.title: Design the retrieval layer for a short-video recommender. How do you blend multiple retrieval sources?
questions.content: Describe the overall retrieval architecture, which sources you would use, and how their results are merged and deduplicated before ranking.
questions.referenceAnswer: Retrieval must reduce tens of millions of items to a few hundred or thousand candidates with high recall and low latency. Typical sources: (1) Collaborative filtering / two-tower embedding retrieval, with user and item towers computed offline and ANN search online. (2) Content-tag retrieval matching user interest tags against item tags. (3) Trending and fresh-item retrieval to handle cold start and exploration. (4) Social-graph retrieval. To merge: take top-k per source under a configurable quota, dedupe by item id, and keep the source as a feature for ranking. Do not attempt fine-grained score fusion at the retrieval layer — leave that to pre-ranking and ranking. Also handle already-seen filtering, diversity spreading, and make per-source quotas configurable so they can be A/B tested.

questions.title: Your model performs far worse online than offline. How do you debug it?
questions.content: Give a systematic debugging approach spanning data, features, model, and infrastructure.
questions.referenceAnswer: First separate 'the metric definitions disagree' from 'the model genuinely regressed'. Then work through: (1) Offline evaluation problems — leakage or an incorrect temporal split inflating offline numbers. (2) Train/serve skew — verify online feature computation matches offline, including feature versions, missing-value handling, and categorical encoding maps. (3) Feature freshness — offline used a feature that is delayed or unavailable at prediction time. (4) Distribution shift — compare online versus offline feature and label distributions. (5) Infrastructure — wrong model version deployed, timeouts falling back to a default policy, or the feature service returning nulls. (6) Measurement — full traffic versus a slice, unbalanced A/B buckets, inconsistent metric definitions. Add feature monitoring and an online-offline consistency check to catch this class of bug earlier.

questions.title: How do you choose the decision threshold for a binary fraud model?
questions.content: Explain what the threshold should be based on, rather than defaulting to 0.5.
questions.referenceAnswer: 0.5 is only sensible when classes are balanced and misclassification costs are symmetric. Start from business cost: estimate the unit cost of a false positive (blocking a legitimate user) and a false negative (letting fraud through), build an expected-cost function, and sweep the threshold on a validation set to find the minimum. If the constraint is operational instead — say manual review can only handle 1000 cases a day — pick the threshold that yields the top-N by score. Two caveats: probabilities must be calibrated first (Platt scaling or isotonic) or the cost math is meaningless, and the threshold needs periodic recalibration because fraud distributions drift.

questions.title: Design a feature platform. How do offline training and online serving share one feature definition?
questions.content: Describe the core components, focusing on how you prevent train/serve skew.
questions.referenceAnswer: The core principle is that a feature is defined once. Components: a feature registry holding the schema and computation logic, offline storage (warehouse) for generating training samples, online storage (low-latency KV) for serving, and a mechanism that compiles the same definition into both batch and streaming execution. Preventing skew: (1) Build training samples with point-in-time correct joins, taking the feature value as of the event time rather than the latest value. (2) Share the same computation code or DSL between offline and online. (3) Run consistency checks before launch, sampling entities and comparing offline versus online feature values. (4) Log the actual feature snapshot used at serving time so you can replay it and reuse it for the next training run.

questions.title: Your RAG system's answer contradicts the retrieved documents. How do you localize the problem?
questions.content: Walk through the layers you would check when RAG output disagrees with the retrieved context.
questions.referenceAnswer: Debug layer by layer. (1) Retrieval — read the top-k documents yourself and confirm the answer is actually in them. If not, it is a recall problem: check whether the embedding model fits the domain, whether chunking split the relevant span, and whether hybrid retrieval (BM25 plus vector) or a reranker is needed. (2) Context assembly — check whether length truncation dropped the key passage, and whether ordering buried the critical evidence in the middle of the context. (3) Generation — check whether the prompt explicitly requires answering only from the provided documents and saying 'I don't know' when unsupported, and whether the model is overriding retrieved content with parametric knowledge. (4) Evaluation — build an evaluation set with citations and measure retrieval recall and generation faithfulness separately, so failures are attributed to a specific stage rather than a vague 'quality is bad'.

questions.title: When should you fine-tune versus use RAG versus prompt engineering?
questions.content: Give the boundaries where each approach applies and the reasoning behind the choice.
questions.referenceAnswer: The decision hinges on whether you are missing knowledge or missing behavior. Missing knowledge — private, time-sensitive, or frequently updated facts — calls for RAG, because the knowledge can be refreshed at any time and answers stay traceable to citations. Missing behavior — a fixed output format, a specific voice, a domain-specific reasoning pattern — calls for fine-tuning, especially when a small set of high-quality examples suffices. Prompt engineering is the right starting point: cheapest, fastest to iterate, and if it solves the problem you should not reach further. The three compose: fine-tuning teaches the model how to use retrieved material, RAG supplies the material itself. The antipattern is fine-tuning to inject facts — expensive, hard to update, and prone to hallucination.

questions.title: How do you evaluate an LLM application? Where do automated and human evaluation each fit?
questions.content: Design an evaluation system for a specific LLM application that can run continuously.
questions.referenceAnswer: Three tiers. (1) Deterministic checks — anything a rule can decide should be a rule: is the output valid JSON, are required fields present, did it trip a safety policy. This tier must be fully automated and run in CI. (2) LLM-as-judge — a stronger model scoring against an explicit rubric, suitable for relevance, faithfulness, and helpfulness. Pin the judge model version, use pairwise comparison to reduce score drift, and periodically calibrate the judge against human labels. (3) Human evaluation — sampled review of final quality, serving as the anchor for the first two tiers. You also need a fixed regression set that runs on every prompt or model change so that fixing A does not silently break B, plus a pipeline that feeds real production failures back into the evaluation set.

questions.title: What is the KV cache, and how does it affect inference memory and throughput?
questions.content: Explain the KV cache mechanism in autoregressive decoding and its resource characteristics.
questions.referenceAnswer: In autoregressive decoding, every generated token attends over the full history. The KV cache stores the keys and values of previous tokens so they are not recomputed each step, reducing per-step cost from O(n^2) to O(n). The cost is memory: cache size equals 2 * layers * heads * head_dim * sequence_length * batch * bytes_per_element, which grows quickly with long context and large batches and can exceed the model weights themselves. Mitigations: MQA/GQA to reduce the number of KV heads, PagedAttention to manage memory in pages and reduce fragmentation, quantizing the cache to int8 or fp8, and sliding-window or compression schemes for very long contexts.

questions.title: Write a function that returns, for each position, the product of all other elements — without using division.
questions.content: Time complexity must be O(n) and space O(1) excluding the output array. Explain your approach and write the code.
questions.referenceAnswer: Two prefix passes. First pass left to right: res[i] holds the product of everything to the left of i. Second pass right to left: keep a running variable for the product to the right and multiply it in. Avoiding division means zeros are handled naturally. Code: res = [1]*n; p = 1; for i in range(n): res[i] = p; p *= nums[i]; q = 1; for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): res[i] *= q; q *= nums[i]; return res. Time O(n), space O(1) excluding output.

questions.title: Implement one iteration of k-means, and explain how you handle empty clusters.
questions.content: Write pseudocode for the assignment and update steps, and explain what to do when a cluster receives no points.
questions.referenceAnswer: Assignment step: for each sample compute the distance to all k centroids and assign it to the nearest. Update step: each cluster's new centroid is the mean of its assigned samples. Empty-cluster strategies: (1) Take the point farthest from all current centroids and make it the new centroid. (2) Split a point off from the largest cluster. (3) Reinitialize that centroid randomly. Without handling it, the mean computation divides by zero and produces NaN, corrupting all subsequent iterations. Worth adding: k-means++ initialization substantially reduces both empty clusters and poor local optima.

questions.title: Tell me about a time a model you owned underperformed after launch.
questions.content: Use the STAR structure to describe the situation, task, action, and result, focusing on what you learned.
questions.referenceAnswer: A strong answer needs: (1) Situation — the business context and the target metric, stated concretely. (2) Task — your specific responsibility, not a vague 'our team'. (3) Action — the heart of the answer, showing a systematic method rather than luck: verify data consistency first, then feature attribution, then localize to a specific feature whose online computation diverged from offline. (4) Result — a quantified outcome; even if the model was never recovered, state the containment action and the mechanism you put in place afterward, such as an online-offline consistency check. The interviewer is assessing your retrospective ability and honesty, so do not deflect blame onto teammates or the data.

questions.title: How do you push back when a PM asks for a metric improvement that isn't technically feasible?
questions.content: Describe your communication strategy and the basis for your decision.
questions.referenceAnswer: The key is translating 'not feasible' into a quantified boundary that can be discussed, rather than a flat refusal. Steps: (1) Confirm the underlying business goal — the metric is usually a proxy, and another path may reach the same goal. (2) State the ceiling of the current approach with evidence: the information content of available features, label quality limits, or a hard latency budget. (3) Offer tiered options — what level is reachable for what investment, with timelines and risks. (4) If they still insist, document the assumptions and risks explicitly, execute their decision, and agree on a mid-point checkpoint. The goal is to supply the basis for a decision, not to make the decision for them.
